newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. makes no inroads on debt lobbying at U.N..
newsitem.headline: U.S. makes no inroads on debt lobbying at U.N..

text.p: The U.S. Congress and the Clinton administration on Friday attempted to convince U.N. members that a plan to pay $819 million in U.S. debt to the United Nations was the best deal they could expect.

But initial efforts faltered with the European Union, Japan and many developing countries saying Washington's proposals were legally unacceptable. One envoy said Japan, with a lower national income than the United States, might end up paying more dues.

U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson and Senator Rod Grams, a Minnesota Republican, met U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan and U.N. ambassadors to explain the plan approved by the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on Thursday.

The proposed legislation demands a series of U.N. reforms, a permanent cut in U.S. payments, an audit of the United Nations by a congressional agency, a ban on large peacekeeping operations and forgiveness of whatever arrears the United States refuses to pay, among many other conditions.
"I think we have made some real progress in building the important role between the U.S. and the United Nations, a role of cooperation and a role of consensus," Grams said.
He said he told Annan that Congress did not want to micro-manage the United Nations but wanted it "to be a very effective and a very efficient agency."
Richardson, at the same news conference, said this was not a "take it or leave it" plan but would include consultations and trips to the capitals of other member states.
But Grams admitted Congress was not going to pay more than $819 million although the United Nations registered a debt of $1.3 billion owed by the United States at the end of 1996.

One European diplomat attending the meetings with Grams and Richardson said: "They got a series of very firm messages. The main point was that it was legally unacceptable and a violation of international agreements."
The debt, diplomats said, was already owed to member states because of their participation in peacekeeping operations that Washington had voted to establish.

Another said that a condition for the payments -- that the United Nations legally forgive any debt Washington refuses to pay -- amounted to preferential payment for the United States and was equally as unacceptable.
"What is the guarantee of future payments," the envoy asked. "We didn't see any in the proposal."
Richardson, in private conversations, indicated the conditions might be somewhat changed in the final version but had little hope for the amount of money raised.

"The United States is happy because of achieving the deal in a domestic context. Hopefully we got through the cocoon that Congress lives in compared to the outside world," said one key ambassador, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
The United States needs the approval of the 185-member General Assembly for its dues reduction plan and debt payment or it could lose its vote in that body.
